 Pinned Updated   Oct. 27, 2026, 1:17 p.m. ET Aaron Boxerman David M. Halbfinger and Leo Sands 
 Here’s the latest. 
 Israelis flocked to the polls in record numbers on Tuesday in a tightly fought election that pits the long-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, against a loose coalition of rivals determined to unseat his right-wing coalition.
 By 6 p.m. local time (12 p.m. Eastern), four hours before polls were scheduled to close, 66.7 percent of voters had cast ballots. It was the highest figure at that point in the day since Israel’s Central Elections Committee began tracking Election Day turnout in two-hour increments in 1973, and nine percentage points higher than at the same time in 2022.
 Turnout appeared to be particularly high, compared with previous elections, among Arab citizens, who make up about a fifth of Israel’s population. By late afternoon, hours before the polls were set to close, turnout in some Arab-majority towns had exceeded the totals from the last election, in 2022.
 The election is Israel’s first since the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, upended the nation and ignited three years of war. It is also widely seen as the most consequential in the country’s history.
 Voters have a choice between two blocs offering starkly different visions. Mr. Netanyahu is seeking re-election at the helm of the most far-right government in Israeli history. His coalition of nationalists and ultra-Orthodox Jews faces an ideologically diverse group of Jewish opposition parties loosely led by Gadi Eisenkot , a former military chief of staff whose son was killed in the Gaza war. Parties representing Arab citizens of Israel also staunchly oppose Mr. Netanyahu’s government.
 Both sides are framing the election as a make-or-break moment for the country. Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition offers the promise of a more religious Israel with an ever-tighter grip over the West Bank and Gaza. His opponents are casting the vote as the last chance to preserve democracy and pull Israel back from the brink of becoming a pariah state under international sanctions.
 Voting will close at 10 p.m. but is unlikely to deliver an immediate verdict on who will be the next prime minister. Opinion polls suggest that Mr. Netanyahu’s allies and rivals are roughly tied, and assembling a governing coalition in Israel’s parliamentary system could take weeks or months .
 Opposition leaders led by Mr. Eisenkot have called for a reckoning over what they call Mr. Netanyahu’s failure to prevent the catastrophic Oct. 7 attacks. They also have pledged to repair Israel’s shattered image abroad , including by cracking down on Israeli extremist violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
 Mr. Netanyahu has resisted the establishment of an independent commission to investigate the Oct. 7 attacks. He has vowed to move ahead with overhauling Israel’s judicial system, a move that critics say could undermine the country’s liberal democracy. And his allies say they hope to permanently entrench Israeli rule in the West Bank and Gaza despite international condemnation.
 The 77-year-old leader has dominated Israeli politics for decades. In recent days, he repeatedly suggested that the country could face annihilation without him in charge.
 Here’s what else to watch:
 Key issues: In a tumultuous campaign , several issues divided Israeli voters. Read more › 
 West Bank and Gaza: As Israelis headed to the polls, Palestinians in the West Bank were under an Israeli military lockdown. Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza cannot vote in Israeli elections, but they may have much to lose if Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition stays in power. Read more ›
 Poll times: Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party said it had asked the Central Election Committee to extend voting hours nationally beyond 10 p.m., an unheard-of move that election officials are unlikely to grant. Likud’s rivals argued that the highly unusual request was intended to sow doubt about the election’s integrity.
 Election integrity: Mr. Netanyahu used racially tinged language to cast suspicion over high turnout among Arab citizens and to encourage his base to go to the polls. Election officials said Tuesday that there had been no indication of widespread irregularities. 
 Trump weighs in: President Trump has endorsed Mr. Netanyahu , praising him as an important partner in the war against Iran and saying anyone else would be the “wrong leader” for Israel. Analysts were skeptical that the U.S. president’s intervention would sway many voters.

 Reporting from Jerusalem
 Relatives of victims of the Oct. 7 attack are running for Parliament. 
 Image Shira Shapiro, right, a candidate for the Yashar party, meeting with Gadi Eisenkot at a roadside bomb shelter where her son died during the October 7 2023 attack, near Reim, Israel, earlier this month. Credit... Nir Elias/Reuters Several people whose relatives were killed or taken hostage in the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, are running for office in Tuesday’s election, the first national vote since the assault, which shook the country’s foundations and ignited its longest war.
 The October 2023 assault looms large over this week’s vote. There are sharp divisions over who was to blame for failing to prevent the worst military, intelligence and policy disaster in Israel’s history.
 About 1,200 civilians and soldiers were killed that day, according to the Israeli authorities, and roughly 250 were taken hostage to Gaza. Many of the family members of hostages held by Hamas rose to prominence as they campaigned for their loved ones in television interviews and at nationwide protests.
 Most of them called for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to take responsibility for the government’s failures of Oct. 7 and to prioritize negotiating the release of the hostages over continued fighting. Others supported Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing government and urged it to keep up the military pressure on Hamas and Israel’s other enemies.
 Parties from across Israel’s political spectrum have recruited candidates from what have become known as the Oct. 7 families. Here are some of the candidates expected to win a seat in Parliament:
 Shira Shapiro is running with Yashar, the centrist party led by Mr. Netanyahu’s main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot. Ms. Shapiro’s son, Staff Sgt. Aner Shapiro, was on leave from the army on Oct. 7 when he attended the Nova music festival, one of the bloodiest targets of the Hamas-led attack. He took shelter in a crowded roadside bomb shelter and stationed himself by the entrance when gunmen attacked it . As the militants hurled grenades inside, Sergeant Shapiro repeatedly caught the grenades and threw them back out, until he was killed, according to surviving witnesses.
 Zvi Mor , the father of a released hostage, Eitan Mor, is running as a candidate for the far-right party Religious Zionism, headed by Bezalel Smotrich. While Eitan was in captivity, Mr. Mor, an educator, founded a forum of right-wing parents of hostages and soldiers who opposed making deals with Hamas and pushed for Israel to defeat the group militarily.
 Omri Ronen , a reserve soldier, is running with the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan. His grandmother, Nira Ronen, was killed in her home in Kfar Aza, one of the border communities worst hit in the October 2023 attack, along with her Filipina caregiver, Angelyn Aguirre. Before Oct. 7, Mr. Ronen had been one of the leaders of a grass-roots group of reservists protesting the government’s plan to overhaul the judiciary. He said in a recent television interview that Mr. Netanyahu, whom he called “Mr. Oct. 7,” must go. “The word responsibility has meaning,” he said.
 Rafael Ben Shitrit , a former mayor of Beit Shean in northern Israel, is in Yisrael Beitenu, a right-wing opposition party led by Avigdor Liberman. Mr. Ben Shitrit used to belong to Mr. Netanyahu’s conservative Likud party, but abandoned it after his son, Staff Sgt. Elroy Ben Shitrit, was killed in battle on Oct. 7 near the Gaza border. He has been an advocate for an independent state inquiry into what went wrong that day. Mr. Netanyahu has refused such an inquiry, and the opposition parties have pledged to establish one if they are elected.
 Sharon Sharabi , also on Yisrael Beitenu’s list of candidates, is the brother of Eli Sharabi, a former hostage who was released from Gaza only to learn that his wife and two teenage daughters had been killed during the Oct. 7 attack. Another brother, Yossi Sharabi, was also taken hostage and killed after 100 days in captivity. Sharon Sharabi campaigned tirelessly for his brothers’ return. When Eli Sharabi was finally released, many Israelis were outraged over how emaciated he looked. “I was shocked,” Sharon said at the time. “I’d been told he would be thin, but I didn’t imagine how thin. It was extreme.”
 Tali Gvili , running with Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party, is the mother of Master Sgt. Ran Gvili, a member of a police counterterrorism unit who was shot and severely wounded in combat on Oct. 7 and then dragged into Gaza. His remains were recovered and returned to Israel in January 2026. The Gvili and Netanyahu families have become close, and the prime minister attended Sergeant Gvili’s state funeral, saying, “Our souls are bound with yours.”
 Michal Hirsch Negri is running with Together, a joint slate led by right-wing politician Naftali Bennett and the centrist Yair Lapid. Ms. Hirsch Negri’s son Maj. Roee Negri was killed fighting in Kibbutz Be’eri near the Gaza border on Oct. 7. Maj. Shahar Varon , a commander in the reserves, is another Together candidate. He fought that day in Kfar Aza, another border community, and later went to fight in Gaza. He was wounded in battle, then went back into Gaza to fight again. “There is life before October 7th, and there is life after,” he wrote recently, adding, “Our government disappeared that morning — but our people showed up instead.”
 Show more Four Ways Israel’s Election Could End. Eventually.
 No party is expected to achieve a clear victory, which means the election will likely only be the first step in determining who will form the next government. Here’s how that might unfold.

 Image Credit... Heedo Abu Laban/The New York Times Oct. 27, 2026, 12:52 p.m. ET Annie Karni 
 Reporting from Washington
 Support for Israel is waning among Democrats in Congress. 
 Image Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel and Speaker Mike Johnson meeting in Washington last year. Credit... Tierney L. Cross/The New York Times For decades, Israel had virtually unanimous support among Republicans and Democrats in Congress, a reflection of a broader consensus in the United States in favor of strong backing for the Jewish state.
 But that consensus began to fray several years ago and has recently threatened to unravel altogether as Democrats have shifted drastically and rapidly from unequivocal support for Israel, reflecting a sea change in Americans’ views.
 Since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the war in Gaza that followed, a growing number of Democrats have been under pressure from younger and progressive voters who are a crucial part of their base.
 Lawmakers have begun rebuking Israel in ways that were once unimaginable. They have pointed to tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians killed in Gaza and focused much of their ire on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, whose actions and policies have left his country diplomatically isolated and who has become a political lightning rod in the United States. That has put at risk the bipartisan support for military aid that Israel has always counted on from American lawmakers.
 A handful of far-right Republicans and libertarians in Congress have also questioned U.S. support for Israel, raising concern about Palestinian deaths and spending American money to defend a far-off ally. But the skepticism is far more widespread among Democrats.
 The midterm elections have been shaped in part by Democratic voters’ mounting hostility toward Israel. Party leaders now view the issue as one of the major fault lines they will have to contend with next year if they win back control of Congress in November.
 Over the past year, almost half of House Democrats voted to cut off aid to Israel . Democratic leaders who have long been staunch allies have said that the U.S.-Israeli relationship needs a fundamental reset , including a rethinking of the 10-year memorandum of understanding that commits billions of dollars of annual security aid to Israel, which will soon expire.
 And Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, who is the highest-ranking Jewish official in the nation, has condemned Mr. Netanyahu on the Senate floor and called for new leadership in Israel.
 In recent weeks, top Democrats in the House and the Senate have proposed legislation that would impose sanctions on Israel for building settlements, making clear to Israeli companies and banks that they could be penalized for ties to such activity.
 Those moves are in line with what lawmakers are hearing from voters.
 A New York Times/Siena national poll conducted in May found that 74 percent of Democratic voters opposed providing additional economic and military support to Israel. A Pew Research Center poll in April found that eight in 10 Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents had an unfavorable view of Israel.

 Reporting from Tel Aviv I’m in a suburb of Tel Aviv, visiting a civil-society-run election “war room,” where volunteers are working to safeguard the integrity of the vote.
 Video Credit Credit... Johnatan Reiss/The New York Times Oct. 27, 2026, 12:21 p.m. ET Aaron Boxerman 
 Reporting from Jerusalem Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party said in a statement that it had asked Israel’s Central Elections Committee to extend voting hours past the scheduled closing time of 10 p.m. The committee has the authority to do so, though it would be a highly unusual move.
 Netanyahu has repeatedly urged his supporters to head to the polls, saying that right-wing strongholds are failing to turn out in sufficient numbers. The party of Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s leading opponent, said it strongly opposed an extension, arguing that Likud made the request in order to sow doubt about the election’s integrity.
 Oct. 27, 2026, 11:50 a.m. ET Johnatan Reiss 
 Reporting from Tel Aviv The election authorities and volunteers seek to counter threats to voting. 
 Image Packing ballots and polling station equipment at the Central Elections Committee’s Logistics Center in Shoham, Israel, this month. Credit... Amir Levy/Getty Images In the run-up to Tuesday’s election Israel, perhaps the country’s most intensely scrutinized vote ever, the authorities and civil society groups mobilized to monitor the balloting, which many fear could be undermined by political interference and disinformation.
 In an office building north of Tel Aviv, dozens of volunteer tech workers and lawyers planned to squeeze into a “war room” to field reports from thousands of volunteers watching polling sites for violence or obstruction. The effort is organized by antigovernment protest groups that say their goal is not to encourage voting for any political party but to ensure safe access to polls.
 In Jerusalem, officials from the Central Election Committee are overseeing an extensive Election Day operation from Parliament. Committee employees are fanning out to more than 12,000 polling stations wearing body cameras to document irregularities. A desk operated jointly with Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, is scanning the web for disinformation to respond to it in real time.
 “This election is the most threatened ever,” said Assaf Shapira, a researcher at the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan think tank. “The stakes are very high,” he said.
 Some experts point to concerns, including the growing sophistication and prevalence of A.I.-generated content, a police force that critics say is increasingly loyal to the far-right minister overseeing it and a sitting Israeli government whose senior officials have repeatedly suggested the vote could be rigged.
 The Central Election Committee, a partly political body chaired by a Supreme Court justice and whose administrative branch is composed of nonpartisan officials, is working to bolster confidence in the process and counter false claims of fraud, Dean Livne, the committee’s acting director general, said in an interview.
 Tallies from each polling station will be made public within hours of the polls closing, and the counting of roughly 600,000 ballots cast remotely at places like hospitals, embassies, and military bases will be live streamed for nearly 24 hours, according to Mr. Livne.
 “This election will be the most transparent ever,” he said.
 Election observers agree that the risk of widespread fraud or manipulation of the vote count is exceedingly low. And as of Tuesday afternoon, election officials said there had been no indication of widespread irregularities. But some experts also say that government officials could be laying the groundwork to undermine confidence in the election so that they can then challenge an unfavorable result as rigged.
 Throughout the campaign, members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party have questioned the impartiality and qualifications of election officials and suggested that antigovernment groups were plotting to obstruct the vote.
 “To challenge the legitimacy of elections, you have to plant the seeds early on,” Yael Shomer, a political scientist at Tel Aviv University, said. “And I think we see them planting the seeds.”
 Senior government officials have stopped short of explicitly threatening to reject the election result. Mr. Netanyahu recently said that he would stand to lose the election if too few of his supporters turned out to vote.
 Observers warn of disinformation campaigns and attempts to intimidate some voters and deter them from casting their ballots on Election Day. 
 Such attempts, opposition figures and some experts worry, could involve the Israeli police, which is increasingly seen as serving the interests of the far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir. Some fear that on Election Day, officers could look the other way at pro-government violence or attempts to intimidate voters outside polling stations in areas considered hostile to Mr. Netanyahu and Mr. Ben-Gvir.
 Israel’s police commissioner, Danny Levy, has vowed to defend the integrity of the vote and said he would dismiss officers who express political views while on duty.
 Concerns about voter intimidation are particularly high for Israel’s Arab citizens, who make up roughly 20 percent of the population and typically vote for parties opposed to Mr. Netanyahu’s. Turnout in Arab communities has historically been low, and they have been targeted with largely unsubstantiated allegations of widespread voter fraud by Mr. Netanyahu and his political allies.
 Earlier this month, Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s far-right finance minister, announced plans to deploy thousands of religious Jewish “observers” to “prevent fraud in voting and vote-counting in Arab communities.” Critics fear that could instigate chaos and discourage Arab citizens from going out to vote.
 Officials in Arab localities are organizing teams to share verified information with their communities to combat disinformation intended to deter voting, including false reports of polling station closures or violence around voting sites, said Abed Shahada, who leads an effort to increase turnout for an organization representing Arab local officials.
 “The threats are greater, but there is also a greater awareness of them,” he said. “We’re trying to have one confront the other.”

 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Oct. 27, 2026, 10:20 a.m. ET Natan Odenheimer and Heedo Abu Laban 
 Reporting from Jerusalem
 Votes from Israel’s Arab citizens could help decide the election. 
 Image A Palestinian citizen of Israel casting a ballot on Tuesday in Umm al-Fahm, Israel. Credit... Mahmoud Illean/Associated Press Arab voters could tip the scales as Israelis turned out in large numbers to vote on Tuesday in one of their country’s most consequential elections in decades.
 Arab citizens, who make up about a fifth of Israel’s population, have historically voted at significantly lower rates than Jewish Israelis in national elections . But pollsters, researchers and activists expected Arab voters to turn out in force, driven to unseat a right-wing government that has enacted aggressive policies against them.
 Arab Israelis are overwhelmingly Muslim, with Druse and Christian communities making up around 15 percent. Palestinians living in the Israeli-occupied West Bank are not Israeli citizens and cannot vote.
 Recent polls suggest that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing alliance nor the opposition bloc is likely to form a majority without a partnership with Arab parties. Such a stalemate would leave Arab leaders with huge influence on the results.
 “The stakes are too high to sit this one out,” said Sireen Jabareen, 30, a director of a rights organization that helps Arab prisoners. She said she would vote for the first time after previously boycotting the political system, which she views as discriminatory toward Arabs. “I don’t want to be the kind of person who clings to rigid principles when reality changes,” she added.
 Many others have also stayed home on Election Day in the past, alienated by political leaders, convinced their ballots hold no sway or unwilling to validate a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens.
 Arab politicians and local leaders are warning of voter-suppression efforts, through either disinformation campaigns or the presence of armed right-wing activists near polling stations in Arab villages.
 Last week, Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party announced a joint effort with another right-wing party to send 2,000 activists to oversee “voting integrity” in Arab cities and towns. The move was widely seen as an attempt to suppress Arab voters.
 In the 2015 election, Mr. Netanyahu sought to prod supporters by saying that Arab voters were “heading to the polls in huge quantities.” After critics accused him of race-baiting, he apologized for any offense caused by the remark.
 But on Tuesday, he tried a similar tactic, pointing to apparently high turnout among Arab voters and suggesting that they were “trying to steal the elections.” (Election authorities said there had been no indication of widespread irregularities.) Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party released a poster showing a crowd of women in hijab, urging right-wing Israelis “not to stay home.” 
 Yousef Makladeh, a leading pollster focusing on Arab society in Israel, said recent surveys indicated that 65 percent to 70 percent of Arab voters planned to vote on Tuesday. That would be an increase of 12 to 18 percentage points over turnout in the 2022 election.
 For the very first time, activists say, efforts to turn out the vote feel like pushing on an open door.
 Omar Abu Siyam, a social media personality from Mu’awiya, an Arab village near Haifa, Israel, said that when he told his nearly 90,000 Instagram followers that he had changed his mind and decided to vote, hundreds of commenters responded that they felt the same way.
 The most critical issue for Arab voters by a wide margin, Mr. Makladeh said, is the surge in violent crime within their communities, a crisis many say the police have deliberately neglected under Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister.
 “Arabs are terrified of what four more years with Ben-Gvir in office will do to us,” said Dr. Thabet Abu Ras, a political geographer who is advising voter-turnout initiatives across Arab municipalities. He added that discriminatory housing policies, resulting in a record number of home demolitions in Arab communities, were also driving voters.
 Higher Arab turnout could threaten smaller parties that are more likely to support Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition. By increasing the total number of votes cast, it would raise the threshold for smaller parties to win seats in the Knesset.
 “This time,” Dr. Abu Ras said, “the Arab vote is worth gold.”

 Reporting from Lod, Israel The high voter turnout seemed apparent in the mixed Jewish-Arab city of Lod, where residents have been waiting in long lines to cast their ballots.
 Video Credit Credit... Heedo Abu Laban/The New York Times Oct. 27, 2026, 9:21 a.m. ET Aaron Boxerman 
 Reporting from Jerusalem The latest update from Israel’s Central Elections Committee said that as of 2 p.m. local time, voter turnout was 44.9 percent — the highest in decades for that time of day and six percentage points more than at the same point in the 2022 general election. Dean Livne, the committee’s acting director, told reporters that there were still long lines at some polling places. Anyone who is waiting in line at 10 p.m., when the polls close, will be allowed to cast a vote, he said.

 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Oct. 27, 2026, 9:10 a.m. ET Isabel Kershner 
 Reporting from Jerusalem
 Why parties with dim prospects get so much airtime in Israel. 
 Image Israeli flags hanging outside a shop in Jerusalem, as the country prepares for national elections. Credit... Kevin Coombs/Reuters Israelis voting on Tuesday will encounter a smorgasbord of ballot slips printed with the initials and names of no less than 36 parties in the election.
 The majority have no chance of making it into the 120-seat Parliament — but a quirk of the Israeli election system ensures that even the most obscure contenders get their moment in the political limelight.
 While parties are barred from buying television time in Israel, they are entitled to seven minutes of free airtime on each of the main television and radio channels — with extra time for every seat that a party holds in the outgoing Parliament. Nightly blocks of election broadcasts, which can run for almost an hour in the two weeks before the ballot, have been a mainstay of campaigns since television arrived here in the 1960s.
 The campaign features about a dozen larger parties that are expected to meet, or come close to, the four-seat minimum threshold to enter Parliament.
 But every Israeli election also includes an array of esoteric parties run by a gamut of characters from would-be messiahs to pranksters. Of the 38 parties that registered with Israel’s Central Elections Committee, two have since dropped out.
 The Pirate Party of Israel has been running in Israeli elections since 2012 on a platform that calls for civil liberties in the digital age as well as free internet and “peace between all the people who live here.” For this election, the party has Dan Ariely — an Israeli American behavioral economist and best-selling author — running in the third slot of its optimistically expansive 24-person slate of candidates.
 Another party, Sharshar for Love and Unity, is led by Eitan Shvili, who cosplays a monarch called King Sharshar in full royal regalia complete with a bejeweled crown and a blue cape. His bid for the premiership, clearly a long shot, comes with a promise of a free theater ticket for every Israeli adult.
 Gan Eden, or Paradise, party wants to build a society based on peace, justice, freedom and plenty. The party has called for reforming the education system to better connect it with spirituality, removing taxes on basic goods and also promoting dialogue between Jews, Muslims, Christians and other communities — a worthy cause but not one that is likely to carry this party of relative unknowns into the Parliament.
 There’s also the Everlasting Covenant for the Salvation of Israel party, which calls for a constitution based on the Torah; and the Bible Bloc, a Jewish-Christian party whose leader, Avi Dennis Lipkin, warns from his living room that Israel must prepare to take in 10 million Jews and non-Jews because of an impending holocaust abroad.
 And in what could be seen as a cynical use of the democratic process, the wife and the mother of the Israeli extremist who assassinated Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in 1995 are leading a party calling for his release from prison. The assassin, Yigal Amir, is serving a life sentence. Israel passed a law in 2001 barring the commutation of a sentence of anyone convicted of assassinating a prime minister, ensuring that Mr. Amir would not be paroled.

 Naftali Bennett, left, and Avigdor Lieberman. Gadi Eisenkot, a former chief of staff for Israel’s military, will likely get the most votes of those hoping to succeed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a pivotal national election on Tuesday.
 But that doesn’t mean that only Mr. Eisenkot could lead a government that unseats the longtime leader.
 Depending on how Israel’s complex coalition-building process shakes out , at least two other veteran politicians could also find themselves vying for the prime minister’s chair: Avigdor Liberman, a hard-right former defense minister, and Naftali Bennett, a onetime prime minister who has fiercely argued in favor of Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
 Opinion polls in recent months have suggested that Mr. Bennett’s party will secure around a dozen seats in Israel’s 120-member Parliament, or Knesset, while Mr. Liberman’s will collect closer to eight. (Mr. Eisenkot’s party could rack up over 20 seats, according to pre-election polls.)
 The political evolutions of Mr. Bennett and Mr. Liberman offer a case study in how Mr. Netanyahu has polarized Israel during his long tenure. The two men should be ideal political partners with the prime minister, as they share many of his hawkish views. Both have worked as advisers to Mr. Netanyahu in the past and even campaigned on his behalf.
 Yet they have long since broken with the Israeli leader, and now accuse him of corruption, abuses of power and a willingness to cut deals with extremists in order to remain in charge. Mr. Netanyahu is currently on trial for corruption in three separate but interlocking cases; he has denied all wrongdoing.
 A veteran of Israeli politics, Mr. Liberman was born in the Soviet Union and leads the right-wing Yisrael Beitenu party. His base is among the hundreds of thousands of Russian-speaking Jews who similarly emigrated to Israel from the former Communist bloc.
 Mr. Liberman lives in the West Bank settlement of Nokdim, and takes a hard-line view on security issues. At one point during the war in Gaza, Mr. Liberman called for Israel to halt all aid, including water, to Palestinians there, even as the enclave faced a humanitarian crisis.
 Mr. Bennett served as prime minister from 2021 to 2022, during the sole hiatus in Mr. Netanyahu’s premiership since 2009. Though his party secured only seven seats in Parliament in the preceding election, Mr. Bennett leveraged the opposition’s desire to unseat Mr. Netanyahu and he went from being kingmaker to king.
 In office, however, Mr. Bennett presided over a fragile, ideologically discordant coalition that ranged from his right-wing Yamina party to Raam, an Islamist party of Arab citizens of Israel. Many of his voters saw his decision to join with left-wing and Arab parties as a betrayal, and as some of his own lawmakers defected, his government collapsed.
 Now, Mr. Bennett is running in alliance with Yair Lapid, a centrist who succeeded him as prime minister in the anti-Netanyahu government. In addition to holding large campaign rallies, Mr. Bennett has released videos of himself holding lengthy, impromptu debates with right-wing voters in the streets and around cafe and restaurant tables.
 In this election, both Mr. Liberman and Mr. Bennett have focused much of their campaign messaging on Israel’s ultra-Orthodox minority.
 The ultra-Orthodox population is 14 percent of Israel’s total but growing rapidly, and they receive far more state benefits than they contribute in taxes, thanks largely to Mr. Netanyahu, who has relied on their support to stay in power. 
 Ultra-Orthodox religious students are also largely exempt from mandatory military service. During the war in Gaza, religious and secular Israelis alike were furious at what they saw as a powerful minority shirking the wartime burden.
 Mr. Bennett has promised to end what he calls an ultra-Orthodox “state within a state” and compel them to participate in national service.
 Mr. Liberman, for his part, has inveighed against what he calls an ultra-Orthodox political push for “us to send our children to the army, to do reserve duty, to work, and pay taxes, while they build their own state.” He has accused them of “trying to dismantle the country.”

Pool photo by Maya Alleruzzo Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel has led the country’s most right-wing government in recent years, with two ultranationalist ministers in particular pushing policies and positions that have exacerbated friction with many of the nation’s traditional allies.
 These politicians, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, who is also responsible for the administration of the Israeli-occupied West Bank, are vocal about expanding Jewish settlements on land that much of the international community considers illegally occupied and designated for a Palestinian state.
 But they are not in the same political party or always on the same page. In this election, they are not running on the same slate, unlike in the two previous votes.
 Mr. Ben-Gvir leads Otzma Yehudit, or the Jewish Power party; and Mr. Smotrich heads the Religious Zionist party. Mr. Smotrich’s party is running this year on a list with the Zehut, or Identity party, led by Moshe Feiglin, a former member of Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party.
 Mr. Ben-Gvir has refused Mr. Netanyahu’s attempts to team him and Mr. Smotrich again in hopes of ensuring the parties clear the threshold of 3.25 percent of votes in Israel’s proportional parliamentary system so that the right-wing bloc does not lose any votes. Mr. Smotrich had expressed reservations, as well.
 Polling shows Mr. Ben-Gvir is popular with young voters , and he is betting he can secure more parliamentary seats for his party and exercise more power in negotiations to form a right-wing government after the election. He told Time magazine on Thursday that he, nevertheless, supports Mr. Netanyahu and aims to push the next government further right.
 Mr. Ben-Gvir is so virulently nationalist that he was not drafted for the Israeli military in his youth. His views were long considered fringe even by other right-wing politicians, like those in Mr. Smotrich’s party.
 In recent years, both ministers have gained power domestically and have become known internationally for inflammatory stances and actions. After the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which ignited a devastating war in Gaza, both called for Israel to adopt destructive policies to encourage the “voluntary emigration” of Palestinians.
 Amid the war, violence by extremist Jewish settlers in the West Bank spiked drastically, and both ministers were accused of encouraging impunity. Last year, Britain, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway imposed sanctions on Mr. Ben-Gvir and Mr. Smotrich for “repeated incitements of violence against Palestinian communities.”
 Israel has in recent years undertaken an unbridled expansion of Jewish settlements while military operations in the West Bank have resulted in the biggest displacement of Palestinian civilians in the territory since the Arab-Israeli war of 1967. Both Mr. Smotrich and Mr. Ben Gvir want to accelerate these efforts.
 Mr. Smotrich has pushed measures extending Israel’s footprint in the West Bank . This year, the security cabinet made it easier for Jews to buy land in parts of the West Bank, and Mr. Smotrich was explicit about his intent. “We are deepening our roots in all parts of the Land of Israel and burying the idea of a Palestinian state,” he said.
 In the election, Mr. Netanyahu faces competition from former military general Ofer Winter, who formed a new right-wing party, People of Israel. Recent polling shows the party is drawing support from Likud even as the opposition presents a significant challenge.
 And Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief who lost a son and two nephews in the war in Gaza, is the leading candidate against Mr. Netanyahu.
 Israelis don’t vote for a prime minister individually, but for a list of candidates presented by a party or parties. The premiership does not automatically go to the party with the most votes, and much more wrangling is needed before it becomes clear who the next leader will be.
 Last year, Mr. Eisenkot formed the party Yashar! — Hebrew for “straight” or “honest” — and has said that he will not serve on a government with Mr. Netanyahu. He says he is running to “save Israel” from endless wars and policies dividing Israelis and destroying its international standing, as well as from Mr. Netanyahu. Polling in the days ahead of the election shows Mr. Eisenkot’s party with a slight lead over Likud, potentially securing more seats in the Knesset, or Parliament, than the prime minister’s party.
 But the Israeli electoral system is complicated and no party has ever won a majority of seats in the Knesset, so there has been much debate and deal-making to build potential future governing coalitions ahead of the vote, and they will continue after the results are in.

Gideon Markowitz/Reuters Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, have emerged as the top candidates to form the next government in Israel after the general election on Tuesday, the country’s first since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks set off the war in Gaza. 
 But other candidates have brought their own drama to the campaign, which has also featured revelations about security failures and a furor over an A.I.-generated political ad.
 Here are some key moments from the campaign.
 An Alliance Underwhelms
 Before Election Day had even been set, the opposition politicians Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, both former prime ministers, announced a joint run for office. The two men have worked together before: They briefly unseated Mr. Netanyahu in 2021, forming a government that lasted less than two years .
 Their announcement in April was seen as mutually beneficial, positioning Mr. Bennett as a candidate for prime minister and ensuring that Mr. Lapid would remain one of the most prominent figures in the anti-Netanyahu bloc.
 But their ambition to make their unified party, B’Yachad, the largest in the Knesset quickly fizzled. Surveys consistently suggest the party will finish in third place.
 An A.I. Video Sparks Anger
 Parties across Israel’s political spectrum have published A.I.-generated content to reinforce their messaging. The content has sometimes stirred up controversy — no more so than in July, when Mr. Netanyahu posted a video depicting Mr. Eisenkot.
 In the video, Mr. Eisenkot is shown running through a meadow, arms open, toward a man with a striking resemblance to his late son Gal, who was killed in 2023 at the start of the Israeli military’s war in Gaza. But he runs past the young man, instead embracing Mansour Abbas , a prominent Arab politician. Mr. Netanyahu has sought to paint Mr. Abbas, who could help Mr. Eisenkot form a governing coalition, as a supporter of terrorism.
 Mr. Netanyahu’s party, Likud, denied that the young man in the video looked like Mr. Eisenkot’s son or was meant to evoke him. But many Israelis reacted to the ad with anger and disgust. Matan Kahana, a former lawmaker running on Mr. Eisenkot’s slate, said there was “no bottom to the pit the Likud is willing to sink into.”
 An Unexpected Partnership
 Image Mansour Abbas, left, and Yoav Segalovitz at a Raam campaign event in Sakhnin, Israel, in September. Credit... Avishag Shaar-Yashuv for The New York Times One of the campaign’s most surprising moments came when Mr. Abbas and Yoav Segalovitz, a veteran Zionist politician and former police commander, announced a joint run. Teaming up on the slate of the United Arab List, or Raam, they offered themselves as an example of Jewish-Arab cooperation, even as they braced for intense criticism from both of their communities.
 “There are people who are afraid of partnership,” Mr. Abbas said. “There are parties that are afraid of partnership. They are afraid of what people will say, afraid of what they will lose. Raam is not afraid of partnership. Raam advances it.”
 A Warning Ignored
 Mr. Netanyahu came under new pressure over reports in the Israeli media and in The New York Times that Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed, the president of the United Arab Emirates, had warned him in advance of Oct. 7, 2023, that Hamas was considering a major attack on Israel.
 The warning from Sheikh Mohammed never reached the leaders of Israel’s security establishment, The Times reported, citing five former senior Israeli officials. Mr. Netanyahu has denied the reports.
 The FlyDubai Attack
 Israelis seemed to forget the election for a day in late September, when the news emerged that a handful of their fellow citizens had stopped a pilot from crashing a FlyDubai commercial jet bound for Tel Aviv.
 Mr. Netanyahu spent hours celebrating the passengers’ resourcefulness, diverting attention away from headlines at the time about his and other officials’ failure to stop the Hamas-led attack in 2023.
 Within days, however, his government was on the defensive over revelations of security failures that had allowed the FlyDubai pilot, an Omani man said to have embraced extreme Islamist views, into the cockpit in the first place.

David Guttenfelder/The New York Times Four years of internal turmoil, war and growing global isolation have left Israelis bitterly divided over their country’s future as they vote in national elections on Tuesday. Opinion polls suggest it will be a close race with the possibility that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party nor his opponents will secure a majority.
 Many Israelis see the election as a choice over whether to continue the rule of the country’s most hard-line, right-wing government ever, and the dominant fault line is Mr. Netanyahu himself. Critics say he has steered Israel to the lowest point in its history, while his supporters see him as an indispensable leader who has tried to destroy Israel’s enemies in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
 Beyond Mr. Netanyahu’s leadership, however, there are plenty of issues polarizing the country.
 Accountability for the Oct. 7 attacks
 The Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, loom over the vote. About 1,200 Israelis were killed in the assault and 250 were seized as hostages, according to the Israeli authorities, making it the deadliest day in Israeli history.
 Israel’s military response in Gaza leveled much of the enclave and killed more than 70,000 people, according to local officials, who do not distinguish between civilians and combatants. Most of the enclave’s two million residents were displaced, often multiple times.
 Three years later, Israelis still have no official answer about why Mr. Netanyahu’s government and the Israeli military failed to foresee the attacks and then struggled to respond even as Hamas fighters invaded villages and a music festival, killing civilians.
 Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents — a bloc of opposition parties and their leaders — have said they would establish an independent inquiry with broad authority, appointed by the president of the Supreme Court. Mr. Netanyahu has called for a “democratic and equitable” commission that would be made of an equal number of representatives of the coalition and the opposition.
 Families of those killed and taken hostage broadly back the opposition, arguing that Mr. Netanyahu’s proposal would politicize what should be a comprehensive and dispassionate investigation.
 The ultra-Orthodox minority
 Secular and liberal Israelis have long been uneasy about the status of the ultra-Orthodox, an insular community that adheres to a fundamentalist interpretation of Jewish scripture and makes up roughly 14 percent of the population. Their religious students are eligible for an exemption from mandatory military service and receive state benefits despite not joining the work force.
 During the wars in Gaza and Lebanon, that long-simmering frustration boiled over into outrage . Hundreds of Israelis from other backgrounds were killed in combat, and hundreds of thousands more did dangerous rounds of reserve duty.
 Mr. Netanyahu’s government has relied heavily on the support of ultra-Orthodox parties. His opponents have called for ending the exemption to the draft for the ultra-Orthodox and cutting off welfare benefits for those who avoid military service.
 Judicial overhaul
 Before the war, Mr. Netanyahu’s government had sought to advance a highly contentious plan to weaken Israel’s judiciary. Critics, including the president of Israel’s Supreme Court, argued that it would fundamentally undermine Israeli democracy.
 Hundreds of thousands of Israelis protested the proposals in mass demonstrations , saying that Mr. Netanyahu was leading the country toward dictatorship.
 The Hamas-led attacks largely suspended the overhaul, part of which was also reversed by a Supreme Court ruling. But Mr. Netanyahu’s allies say they will push ahead with the changes if they are re-elected.
 The Palestinians
 While global attention has focused on the West Bank and Gaza, domestically both Mr. Netanyahu and his opponents have preferred to focus elsewhere. Mr. Netanyahu and most of his leading rivals say they oppose giving the Palestinians an independent state.
 They still offer different visions for the near future.
 Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition is dominated by religious nationalists who have advanced Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank at a breakneck pace. They have called for Israel to urge Palestinians to leave Gaza, with one senior minister saying conditions there should be kept miserable to “take away their hope.”
 The fractious bloc of parties opposing Mr. Netanyahu hold wildly diverging views on the Palestinians. They include the left-wing Democrats party, whose members generally support a two-state solution but would have limited influence in a future coalition.
 Gadi Eisenkot, who opinion polls suggest will lead the alliance, has vowed to rein in Israeli extremist attacks on Palestinians and engage on the Trump administration’s cease-fire plan for Gaza . But Mr. Eisenkot also supports some Israeli settlements in the West Bank and has even attacked Mr. Netanyahu for having once supported a Palestinian state.
